## What will you be able to do?

::: {.key-idea}
Open a small project, run its code, and explain why the result appears.
:::

::: {.incremental}

- Find the project's inputs and code.
- Run a script and a notebook.
- Explain a relative path and a notebook's memory.
- Review one small change proposed by an agent.

:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 01:00–03:00 (2 minutes). State the observable destination: every student
will produce Monthly saving (EUR): 200 and explain where it came from.
The hour has four parts: orient 0–15, scripts and paths 15–33, notebooks 33–46,
and an agent demonstration plus exit check 46–60. Later blocks teach Python
syntax, Git, and pandas in depth. Do not introduce those workflows here.
:::

## A project is a folder with a purpose

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {.project-tree}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
lecture-1/
├── README.md
├── household_saving.py
├── project_running.ipynb
├── data/
│   └── raw/
│       └── households.csv
└── outputs/
```
:::

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

- **Instructions:** how to run the project.
- **Code:** the steps of the calculation.
- **Data:** the supplied inputs.
- **Outputs:** generated results.

:::
:::

::: {.small-note}
Today's script uses two numbers written in the code. We will read the CSV later.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 03:00–05:00 (2 minutes). Show the real folder tree, not just this diagram.
Explain the filename extensions: .md is readable text, .py is Python source,
.ipynb is a notebook, .csv is a plain-text data table. The CSV contains four
invented households; no real people's data. Outputs is a destination for later
tables and figures; this lesson prints to the screen. The README in outputs is
only a placeholder. Locate codes/lecture-1 in the course repository once, then
use that starter folder as the project root throughout this hour.
:::

## Open the project root

1. Open the supplied **`codes/lecture-1`** folder.
2. Find `README.md`, the script, and the notebook.
3. Keep these files together in that folder.

::: {.definition}
The **project root** is the main folder of the project we are running.

For this lesson, it is the folder called `lecture-1`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 05:00–07:00 (2 minutes). The common setup starts JupyterLab from this
folder. In a prepared terminal at the course repository root, demonstrate
cd codes/lecture-1 followed by jupyter lab. If a student has the standalone
starter folder, open it directly and do not repeat that relative cd command.
Do not ask beginners to clone a repository before the Git block. Remind them
to extract a downloaded ZIP before opening or running its contents.
:::

## Three tools, three jobs

| Tool | What you do there | Today's example |
|---|---|---|
| Text editor | Read, change, and save a file | `household_saving.py` |
| Notebook | Combine explanation, code cells, and output | `project_running.ipynb` |
| Terminal | Ask the computer to run a command | `python household_saving.py` |

::: {.key-idea}
JupyterLab gives us all three in one workspace.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 07:00–09:00 (2 minutes). Show all three tabs in the actual interface.
Double-click the .py file to open the text editor, double-click the .ipynb file
to open the notebook, and use File > New > Terminal for the terminal. A terminal
shell prompt and a notebook cell accept different kinds of instructions.
The browser is the interface to the local JupyterLab server; opening it does
not by itself upload their project. Keep the prepared Python environment active.
:::

## Check that Python is available

In the prepared **terminal**, type:

```bash
python --version
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Python 3.12.x
```
:::

::: {.small-note}
The last number may differ. Use the course environment; ask for help if the command fails.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 09:00–11:00 (2 minutes). Explain that Python is the program executing our
instructions. The x on the slide stands for a patch version, not literal output.
If necessary, activate the prepared research-methods environment. In the
notebook choose its Python 3 kernel. Do not turn this into an installation
session; use a prepared working setup and arrange follow-up help. The terminal
command itself is not Python code to paste into an ordinary notebook cell.
:::

## Your turn · Find the pieces

::: {.exercise}
**Four minutes, in pairs.**

1. Find the starter project root and open its README.
2. Open the script in the editor and the notebook in another tab.
3. Open a terminal and check the Python version.

Point to the code, the raw data, and the outputs folder.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
The script and notebook sit beside the README. The CSV is inside `data/raw/`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 11:00–15:00 (4 minutes, including feedback). Circulate. Ask one student
to distinguish the course repository root from this lesson's project root.
Check both students can locate a file. Before continuing, make sure the terminal
is in codes/lecture-1, as explained in the starter README. Reveal the answer
only after students have looked for the files. This is a navigation exercise,
not a test of commands they have not learned.
:::

## Run the script from the project root

In the **terminal**:

```bash
python household_saving.py
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Monthly saving (EUR): 200
```
:::

::: {.definition}
A **script** is a saved sequence of instructions. Python runs this file from top to bottom.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 15:00–18:00 (3 minutes). Run the supplied script. Ask students to identify
the command, file being run, and output as three different things. Explain that
the file extension .py is part of its name, and that a terminal command starts
a new Python process each time. It does not inherit the notebook's variables.
Have everyone obtain the baseline output before changing any code.
:::

## Read this tiny program

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3|5"}
income = 1000
consumption = 800
saving = income - consumption

print("Monthly saving (EUR):", saving)
```

::: {.key-idea .fragment}
EUR 1,000 of income − EUR 800 of consumption = **EUR 200 saved per month**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 18:00–20:00 (2 minutes). Reveal the inputs, calculation, and print line in
that order. These are synthetic amounts for one household and one month.
Say that equals stores a value under a name; the next block will teach variables
systematically. The script's opening docstring is explanatory text and is
omitted from the slide. Do not introduce types, functions, or dataset operations.
:::

## Predict → change → save → run

::: {.exercise}
**Four minutes.** Change income from `1000` to `1200`.

1. Predict saving before running anything.
2. Save the script in the editor.
3. Run `python household_saving.py` again.
4. Compare the output with your prediction.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
`1200 - 800 = 400`. The output should report **EUR 400 per month**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 20:00–24:00 (4 minutes, including debrief). Make students say or write 400
before running. If the old value appears, first check that the editor was saved
and that the terminal is running this same copy of the file. Do not suggest
random reinstallations. Ask students to restore income to 1000, save, and rerun
before moving on. Distinguish saving a file from running the saved file.
:::

## A path starts somewhere

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Absolute path

Starts at a drive or filesystem root.

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
C:/course/lecture-1/
```

Specific to where you stored the project.

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Relative path

Starts at the **current working folder**.

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
data/raw/households.csv
```

Works on another computer if the folder structure is kept.

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 24:00–26:00 (2 minutes). The absolute path is a Windows example, not a path
students must create. macOS and Linux paths begin with /. Explain that / means
go into a folder in the examples. Forward slashes work in these Python paths
on Windows as well. Avoid typing user-specific home directories. Relative
paths help portability but still require the correct working folder.
:::

## Same file, different starting folder

| Current working folder | Relative path to the CSV |
|---|---|
| `lecture-1/` | `data/raw/households.csv` |
| `lecture-1/data/` | `raw/households.csv` |
| `lecture-1/outputs/` | `../data/raw/households.csv` |

::: {.definition}
`..` means **go up one folder**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 26:00–28:00 (2 minutes). Point to the starter tree. Trace each route with
a finger. In the last row go up from outputs into lecture-1, then down through
data and raw. All three paths identify the same existing CSV. Python does not
automatically resolve a relative file path from the folder containing the
script; the working folder is what matters for these ordinary paths.
:::

## “File not found” can mean “wrong starting folder”

Run these cells in the **notebook**:

```python
from pathlib import Path
Path.cwd()
```

```python
Path("data/raw/households.csv").is_file()
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
The working folder should end in `codes/lecture-1`. The file check should return **`True`**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 28:00–30:00 (2 minutes). Open the first two code cells of the supplied
notebook. Demonstrate Shift+Enter now; explain the shortcut more fully in the
notebook section. Path.cwd() displays the kernel's actual current folder.
The displayed path is system-specific and may end only in lecture-1 for a
standalone starter copy. If the check is False, compare cwd with the folder
tree, filename, and extension. We are checking existence, not reading data.
Path is a tool provided by Python; its import syntax is not assessed here.
:::

## Your turn · Choose the right path

::: {.exercise}
**Three minutes.** Your current working folder is `lecture-1/outputs/`.

Which path reaches the raw CSV? Explain each step.

**A.** `data/raw/households.csv`\
**B.** `../data/raw/households.csv`\
**C.** `../households.csv`
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
**B.** Go up to `lecture-1`, then into `data/raw`, then select `households.csv`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 30:00–33:00 (3 minutes). This is a paper or pair discussion exercise;
students need not change their live working folder. A would look for a data
subfolder inside outputs. C would look for the CSV directly in lecture-1.
Reveal B only after explanations. Keep the notebook kernel in the project root
for the next activity so that later cells run without another directory change.
:::

## A notebook combines explanation and code

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Markdown cell

Explains the question, units, and interpretation.

“Saving is income minus consumption, in EUR per month.”

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Code cell

Sends instructions to Python.

```python
saving = income - consumption
print(saving)
```

:::
:::

::: {.key-idea}
Select a cell and press **Shift + Enter** to run it and move to the next cell.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 33:00–35:00 (2 minutes). Show a Markdown cell and a code cell in the live
notebook. Execute the input, calculation, and display cells in order. The
excerpt on this slide assumes the input cell was already run. Point out the
output area and execution counts. Editing code alone does not execute it.
Markdown is explanatory text; its cell is rendered, rather than sent to Python.
:::

## The kernel remembers what ran

::: {.definition}
The **kernel** is the running Python process behind the notebook.
It remembers values created by executed cells.
:::

::: {.incremental}

- Cells can be run in any order.
- Changing text does not update a remembered value.
- The order on the screen can differ from the order you ran.

:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 35:00–37:00 (2 minutes). Contrast this long-lived kernel with the fresh
process started by each python household_saving.py terminal command. Execution
counts record execution order, not an obligation to follow the page. An output
saved in the notebook is a record of a past execution, not proof of current
state. Restarting clears remembered variables but does not edit source cells.
:::

## Same notebook, a stale calculation

::: {.path-label}
First run all three cells with income `1000`. Then change and rerun only the input cell:
:::

```python
income = 1200
consumption = 800
```

::: {.path-label}
Skip the calculation cell, which previously computed `saving = 200`:
:::

```python
saving = income - consumption
```

::: {.path-label}
Rerun only the display cell. What appears?
:::

```python
print("Monthly saving (EUR):", saving)
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
**200.** Updating `income` did not rerun the calculation of `saving`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 37:00–39:00 (2 minutes). Show this exact sequence live. Begin from the
baseline notebook run so saving already exists and equals 200. Edit income to
1200, execute that input cell, then execute the display cell while skipping the
calculation cell. The displayed source looks sensible but the output is stale.
Ask for 200 versus 400 before revealing the answer. State clearly that a Python
assignment stores a value; it does not create a continuously updating formula.
:::

## Your turn · Make the hidden state visible

::: {.exercise}
**Three minutes.** In your own notebook:

1. Start with income `1000`; run inputs, calculation, and display.
2. Change income to `1200`; rerun **only the input cell**.
3. Skip the calculation cell and rerun **only the display cell**.

Explain why the displayed saving is still `200`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 39:00–42:00 (3 minutes). Students reproduce the demonstration themselves.
If they see 400, check whether they ran the calculation cell as well. If they
see NameError, the baseline calculation was never run in this kernel; run the
three cells once at income 1000, then repeat. Both outcomes reveal execution
history. Leave the edited income at 1200 for the clean rerun on the next slide.
:::

## Restart, then run every cell in order

In JupyterLab, choose:

**Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells…**

::: {.key-idea}
A clean run clears the remembered values and rebuilds them from the notebook's cells.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
With income `1200` and consumption `800`, the complete run gives **400**.
:::

Save the notebook after checking its new output.

::: {.notes}
Clock 42:00–45:00 (3 minutes). Ask for the expected result first, then restart
and run all. The menu wording may differ slightly by version. This action
reruns every cell, including imports and the path check; no variable from a
previous session should be needed. It executes the current notebook cells;
save source edits before sharing. Restore income to 1000, restart and run all
again, check saving 200 and the path check True, then save. Restarting checks
execution order, not whether the economic formula is right.
:::

## Saved output records an earlier run

- A `.py` file stores instructions.
- A `.ipynb` file can store instructions **and displayed output**.
- Reopening a notebook does not recreate its remembered variables.

::: {.key-idea}
Read the code, rerun it from a fresh start, and check the calculation.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 45:00–46:00 (1 minute). Separate three checks: can it run, can it run from
a clean start, and does it calculate what we intend? All three matter. Explain
that a beautiful saved output could be old. The CSV is still untouched. This
bridges notebook state to reviewing an agent's change; do not repeat the full
reproducibility lecture scheduled for Day 2.
:::

## One small task for an agent

::: {.key-idea}
Add **saving as a share of income** to the existing script.
:::

For the baseline household:

**EUR 200 saved / EUR 1,000 income = 0.2 = 20%.**

::: {.definition}
We choose the calculation and its check before asking the agent to change code.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 46:00–48:00 (2 minutes). Use the supported classroom agent. Confirm the
script has been restored to income 1000 and consumption 800. Explain that the
agent proposes a code change; the student remains responsible for checking it.
The new quantity is a share, not EUR. This demo is limited to positive income;
zero-income handling comes later with conditions. If the live tool is
unavailable, use the exact proposed change on the review slide as a fallback.
:::

## Give the agent a bounded request

::: {.exercise}
Edit **only `household_saving.py`**.

For the positive income already supplied, append the saving share:
**`saving / income`**. Print it with a clear label.

Keep the existing inputs and saving output. Do not read or write data files,
install packages, or change other files.

Show the proposed change and explain it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 48:00–49:00 (1 minute). Submit this request to the classroom agent after
showing the task to students. Name the file explicitly and ask for a small
change. Do not delegate the entire course project. Point out the requested
formula, preserved behaviour, limited scope, and review step. Wait for the tool
only within this short demo; use the prepared example if necessary.
:::

## Review the proposed change

The original calculation stays. A suitable addition is:

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|2"}
saving_share = saving / income
print("Share of income saved:", saving_share)
```

Before accepting:

- Is the denominator **income**?
- Are the inputs and original output preserved?
- Is only the requested file changed?

::: {.notes}
Clock 49:00–51:00 (2 minutes). Open the actual proposed edits and read them.
If it differs from this example but satisfies the request, assess the actual
behaviour rather than demanding identical syntax. Point out that a diff shows
what changed. Git concepts will be taught later; a side-by-side editor view is
enough here. Reject or correct an unrelated refactor, dependency addition, or
wrong denominator before accepting. The input-domain restriction is explicit.
:::

## Check the agent's result by hand

| Income, EUR/month | Consumption, EUR/month | Saving | Saving / income |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 800 | 200 | 0.20 = 20% |
| 2,000 | 1,500 | 500 | 0.25 = 25% |

::: {.exercise}
**Three minutes, including the demonstration.** Run both cases and compare.

What would `200 / 800 = 0.25` measure in the first case?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Saving relative to **consumption**. That is a different denominator and a different question.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 51:00–54:00 (3 minutes). Run the accepted script with both input pairs.
Check the printed level and share, not merely whether the program exits.
The second household distinguishes the cases and makes checking concrete.
Explain that two hand checks support this small demo; they do not prove
correctness for every possible input. Restore income 1000 and consumption 800
afterwards. Students observe or run the accepted edit if access permits; the
longer practice in agent supervision is scheduled for Day 2.
:::

## If the project will not run, narrow the problem

| Symptom | First check |
|---|---|
| `python` is not found | Is the course environment active? |
| Python cannot open the script | Are you in the starter folder? Is the filename right? |
| Your edit has no effect | Did you save and run the same file? |
| A notebook shows an old value | Did you rerun the calculation? Restart and run all. |
| `NameError` in a notebook | Was the cell defining that name run first? |

::: {.notes}
Clock 54:00–56:00 (2 minutes). Read the actual error, including the filename
and line number when supplied. Do not attempt the full traceback lesson here.
Use one symptom from the room. Ask students to name one diagnostic action at
a time. An error is evidence about a particular step; repeatedly asking an
agent to fix everything makes the investigation harder to follow.
:::

## Exit check · Can someone else run your work?

::: {.exercise}
**Three minutes, individually.**

1. Run the script with the original inputs: saving should be **200**.
2. Restart and run the notebook: saving should be **200** and the path check **`True`**.
3. Explain why a relative path needs a starting folder.
4. Explain why a notebook can display an out-of-date result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 56:00–59:00 (3 minutes). The agent-edited script may also print the share
0.2; its original saving output must remain. Check that the notebook input was
restored to 1000 before the final run. Ask for short independent explanations:
relative paths start from cwd; stored values change only when the relevant
calculation runs. Students should save their files. Record setup issues for
follow-up without extending the hour. No Git commit is required in this block.
:::

## Ready for basic Python {.section-slide background-color="#E85D4A"}

Find the files. State the calculation. Run the code. Check the result.

Next: variables, values, and the steps behind the program.

::: {.notes}
Clock 59:00–60:00 (1 minute). Return to the first slide's goal. Students now
have a runnable project and an experience of both visible source and hidden
execution state. The next block supplies the Python foundations for explaining
each line in more detail. End on time.
:::
